newsitem.title: GERMANY: EURO LAUNCH COULD BOOST FOREX VOLATILITY - BERGSTEN.
newsitem.headline: EURO LAUNCH COULD BOOST FOREX VOLATILITY - BERGSTEN.

text.p: Volatility among key currencies could increase substantially when Europe's euro currency is launched, requiring new forms of international cooperation, U.S. presidential advisor Fred Bergsten said on Wednesday.

The future single currency will be the most important development in the international monetary system since flexible exchange rates in the early 1970s, Bergsten, a key advisor to President Bill Clinton on foreign exchange matters, said.

"A successful euro will be the first real competitor to the dollar since the dollar surpassed sterling as the world's dominant currency in the inter-war period," he told Reuters ahead of a conference of German opposition Social Democrats.
As much as $1 trillion of international investment may shift from dollars into euros, Bergsten, director of the Institute for International Economics, forecast.

The euro, due to start in January 1999, could lead to a bipolar currency regime dominated by Europe and the United States, with Japan as a junior partner. This would replace the dollar-centric system and require a quantum jump in trans-Atlantic cooperation, he said.
In the longer run, the dollar-euro exchange rate is likely to fluctuate considerably more than the dollar has against individual European currencies in the past, he added.
Bergsten said it was not crucial whether the euro starts in 1999 or 2001, or whether Italy, Portugal and Spain are in at the start of economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The same conclusions will apply," he said. "Germany will not let EMU happen unless it is assured of a strong euro."
The United States and the rest of the world should rebuff any European effort to seek any substantially under-valued start-up rate for the euro, Bergsten said.

Such efforts "would represent a blatant European effort to export part of its currently high unemployment and to enable the euro to become a strong currency without any significant costs to the competitive position of the European countries," he commented.
Bergsten said he believed that a more structured exchange rate regime would be needed to manage the relationships between the dollar, the euro and the yen.
The emergence of a more attractive alternative to the dollar could reduce the ability of the United States to finance its large external deficits, he added.
